messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 40
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 49

He is 40, a married Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life learning how to stay steady in crisis. As a surgeon, he is used to moving toward injury while others step back. He trusts routines, sterile fields, and the discipline of his hands. Before the disaster, he describes himself as intense but dependable, the person in his family who remained calm, who made plans, who fixed what could be fixed. He and his wife have built a life around long hospital hours, late dinners, and the shared understanding that his work carries pressure. He takes pride in being the one people rely on.

The earthquake happens on a humid afternoon while he is in the operating room. At first he thinks it is a tremor from faulty equipment, some vibration passing through the floor. Then the overhead lights begin to sway, metal instruments rattle against the tray, and someone shouts. The room lurches hard enough that he has to grab the edge of the table to keep his balance. For a few seconds, training takes over. He hears himself giving instructions, telling the team to protect the patient, to get low, to move carefully. But the walls groan, ceiling tiles drop, and somewhere beyond the operating room he hears a crashing sound followed by screams that do not stop when the shaking does.

In the hours that follow, the hospital becomes unrecognizable. Power cuts in and out. Hallways fill with dust, blood, and people calling names. He works without fully understanding time, moving from one injured body to another. There are too many patients, not enough supplies, and no way to make the choices feel humane. A child arrives blue and limp in her father’s arms. A nurse he knows is trapped under debris before she is pulled free. He remembers the smell of ruptured gas lines and concrete powder settling onto skin like ash. He does not know until much later that his wife has survived with only minor injuries. During those first hours, he is certain he may never see her again.

For weeks afterward, he tells the story like someone describing a long shift. He returns to work quickly because it seems impossible not to. The hospital needs him, and he needs the structure. At home, though, his wife notices that he no longer sits with his back to the window. He checks exits in restaurants. If a truck passes and makes the floor vibrate, his body stiffens before he knows why. At night he sleeps in fragments. He wakes with his heart pounding, already standing beside the bed, convinced for a moment that the walls are moving. Sometimes he dreams he is back in the operating room and his gloves are slick, but when he reaches for the patient, the table is empty.

He becomes more irritable than he has ever been. In the hospital he snaps at residents for small mistakes, then feels ashamed and withdraws. He avoids the wing that was most damaged, taking longer routes through the building even when he is late. He tells himself this is practical, but his chest tightens whenever he nears the cracked stairwell that has since been repaired. He has difficulty concentrating during charting and reads the same line several times before it makes sense. During surgery, he remains technically precise, yet he is unnerved by sudden noises—the clang of a dropped instrument, the slam of a door. Each sound sends a flash through him, a full-body jolt that he masks by becoming even more controlled.

At home, his world gets smaller. His wife wants to talk about moving to a different neighborhood, maybe even leaving the city, but he shuts down when she raises it. He does not want to discuss the earthquake, and he does not want to hear other people’s stories either. Family gatherings feel loud and chaotic. He starts declining invitations, saying he is on call. Their marriage grows quieter. She tells him he is present in the room but far away. He knows she is right. He watches her while she sleeps because part of him still expects everything solid to disappear overnight.

What troubles him most is the change in how he sees himself. He has built his identity around competence, but now he second-guesses ordinary decisions. He thinks about the patients he could not save and the split-second choices he made when resources ran out. He tells himself any surgeon in that situation would have done the same, yet the thought does not settle. On his days off, he tries to run, to read, to help his son with homework, but his attention drifts back to the sound of concrete breaking and voices calling from under rubble. News footage of storms, collapsed buildings, or emergency rescues catches him before he can look away, then leaves him sweating and restless.

Months later, the city appears rebuilt in ways that make other people hopeful. He notices repaired walls, reopened shops, new paint. He also notices the hairline cracks no one else seems to see. He continues to work, continues to operate, continues to function in the way others admire. But beneath that surface he lives as if the ground might shift again at any moment, and some part of him remains in that operating room, listening for the first tremor.
